newsitem.title: PERU: Tokyo envoy tells Fujimori to press ahead on talks.
newsitem.headline: Tokyo envoy tells Fujimori to press ahead on talks.

text.p: A top envoy from Tokyo urged Peru's President Alberto Fujimori to move faster on talks to free 72 hostages held by Marxist guerrillas in the Japanese ambassador's residence.

Amid signs Japan was worried about hawkish voices in the Peruvian military urging a violent foray into the besieged house, Vice Foreign Minister Masahiko Komura met for two hours with Fujimori in the presidential palace.
With negotiations making scant progress, speculation has grown that Fujimori may tire of talking and try to storm the mined and booby-trapped diplomatic compound.

Komura said he asked Fujimori to respond to proposals by a three-man mediation panel, known as the guarantors commission, to resolve the 91-day standoff peacefully. He did not say what those proposals were.
"I asked President Fujimori to respond to efforts by the guarantors commission," Komura said through a translator.

"I asked the president to respond to some petitions with regard to the MRTA," he told reporters, referring to the Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement, which stormed the house during a cocktail party on Dec. 17 and took all the guests hostage.
Tokyo has insisted from the beginning that the lives of the hostages, including its ambassador to Peru and some two dozen VIP Japanese businessmen, must be saved at all costs.
Komura's visit seemed to be aimed at reaffirming that message, while trying to keep those calling for force at bay and urging Fujimori to speed up talks.
"The guarantors commission has tried to persuade both sides to accelerate the negotiations, and he (Komura) was calling on the government to respond to that," a Japanese embassy spokesman said.

Another Japanese diplomat said Komura went to Lima to remind Fujimori of his commitment to end the standoff peacefully, a pledge he made at a meeting with Japan's Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto in Canada in January.

The main reason for Komura's three-nation visit to Latin America was to arrange for asylum in Cuba and the Dominican Republic for all or some of the rebels in exchange for handing over the hostages unharmed, the diplomat said.
Such a provision would be a crucial part of any deal with MRTA to free the hostages. Fujimori went to Cuba last month to arrange an asylum deal with Cuban leader Fidel Castro.

"There are many purposes to this visit but the emphasis is on Cuba and the Dominican Republic, where Mr Komura will visit this week. First he must discuss the issue in Peru with the parties concerned," he told Reuters.
Komura also handed Fujimori a letter from Hashimoto asking him to redouble efforts to solve the standoff peacefully, local radio reports said.

The envoy was not expected to have any direct contact with the Cuban-inspired MRTA, which demands freedom for about 450 jailed comrades in exchange for the hostages. After meeting with the hostages' family members at a Japanese cultural centre late Tuesday, he was due to fly to Havana on Wednesday.

Two of the three mediators, Canadian Ambassador Anthony Vincent and Red Cross official Michel Minnig, later met MRTA leaders at a safehouse across the street from the residence for at least two hours.

The army said Tuesday it captured 38 "MRTA terrorists" and a small arsenal of weapons, including 10 AKM rifles and 11 grenades, in a sweep through eastern Junin department, the only area in Peru outside of the Japanese residence where MRTA still has an armed presence.
The captured group had planned to attack an army base in the town of Oxapampa, an army statement said.

The rebels released most of their 500 captives within a few days of blasting their way in but hold on to the VIPs that include Fujimori's brother Pedro and two of his ministers. Of the 72 hostages, 24 are Japanese citizens, one is Bolivian and the rest are Peruvian.
